m: unfortunately, as bad luck would have it
s: 週末に海へ行く予定だったが、あいにく台風が来て中止になった。
en: We planned to go to the beach at the weekend, but unfortunately a typhoon came and it was called off.
why: あいにく means unluckily, at a bad time for you: 運悪く says the same in plainer words.
予想どおり means 'just as expected'. あいにく says nothing about expecting it, only that it was bad luck.
久しぶりに means 'for the first time in a while'. あいにく is not about how often.
急に means 'suddenly'. あいにく is about bad luck, not speed.
tell: あいにく = 運悪く／残念なことに: bad luck, bad timing.

s: 会議の途中で、部長がいきなり席を立って部屋を出ていった。
en: In the middle of the meeting, the manager suddenly stood up and walked out of the room.
why: いきなり means suddenly, with no warning: 突然 is the plain word for the same thing.
静かに means quietly. いきなり is about no warning, not about noise.
ゆっくり means slowly, close to the opposite of a sudden move.
わざと means on purpose. いきなり says nothing about intent.
tell: いきなり = 突然: without any warning.

s: この辺りには、かつて大きな自動車工場があった。
en: There was once a big car factory around here.
why: かつて means 'once, at some time in the past', and suggests it is gone now: 以前 is the everyday word.
たしか means 'if I remember right'. It is about the speaker's memory, not the time.
長年 means 'for many years'. It gives a length of time, not 'formerly'.
すでに means 'already'. It says something happened earlier than expected, not that it belongs to the past.
tell: かつて = 以前／昔: once, in the past, but not now.

s: 電車の中で、隣の席の人がさっきからしきりに時計を見ている。
en: On the train, the person next to me has been checking the time again and again.
why: しきりに means again and again, over and over: 何度も says it plainly.
じっと means staring without moving. しきりに is many separate looks, not one long one.
こっそり means secretly. しきりに is about how often, not whether anyone notices.
不安そうに describes a feeling. しきりに only says it keeps happening, whatever the mood.
tell: しきりに = 何度も: over and over, again and again.

s: 大事な契約なので、サインする前に内容をじっくり読んでください。
en: This is an important contract, so please read it carefully before you sign.
why: じっくり means slowly and carefully, taking your time: 時間をかけて says the same.
急いで means in a hurry, the opposite of じっくり.
声に出して means reading aloud. じっくり is about time and care, not voice.
もう一度 means one more time. じっくり is about one careful reading, not a repeat.
tell: じっくり = 時間をかけて: slowly, carefully, thoroughly.

s: 三か月続いた駅前の工事がようやく終わり、道が通りやすくなった。
en: The roadworks in front of the station, which went on for three months, are finally over, and the street is easier to get through.
why: ようやく means 'at last, after a long wait or effort': やっと is the everyday word.
思ったより早く means 'sooner than expected', close to the opposite of ようやく.
予定どおり means 'on schedule'. ようやく says the wait felt long, not that it kept to the plan.
いったん means 'for now, for a moment'. ようやく is about the long wait before the end.
tell: ようやく = やっと: at last, after a long wait.

s: 急いで駅に向かったが、最終電車はとっくに出たあとだった。
en: I hurried to the station, but the last train had left long before.
why: とっくに means 'long ago, well before now': ずっと前に says it plainly.
ちょうど here means 'just', a moment before. とっくに is the opposite: long before.
予定どおり means 'on schedule'. とっくに says nothing about the timetable.
なぜか means 'for some reason'. とっくに is about time, not cause.
tell: とっくに = ずっと前に: long since, well before now.

m: for now, for the time being
s: 「もう遅いし、続きは明日にして、今日はひとまず帰ろうよ。」
en: It's late, so let's leave the rest until tomorrow and go home for now.
why: ひとまず means 'for now, as a first step', with more to come later: とりあえず is the everyday word.
まっすぐ means going straight home without stopping. ひとまず is about 'for now', not the route.
急いで means in a hurry. ひとまず says nothing about speed.
一緒に means together. ひとまず says nothing about who goes.
tell: ひとまず = とりあえず: for now, until the next step.

s: 会議で使う資料は、あらかじめ参加者全員にメールで送っておきます。
en: We will email the meeting materials to all participants in advance.
why: あらかじめ means beforehand, before the event: 前もって says the same in plainer words.
後で means later. あらかじめ is before, the opposite.
まとめて means 'all at once, in one go'. It is about how, not when.
念のため means 'just in case'. It gives a reason, not a time.
tell: あらかじめ = 前もって: before the event, in advance.

s: 暑い中、一日中外で作業をしたので、帰るころにはぐったりしていた。
en: I worked outside all day in the heat, so by the time I went home I was completely worn out.
why: ぐったりする means so tired that your body goes limp: とても疲れていた is the plain version.
いらいらする means irritated. ぐったり is about having no energy, not about mood.
お腹がすく means hungry. A long hot day can cause both, but ぐったり means worn out.
日に焼ける means getting sunburned or tanned. That is about skin, not tiredness.
tell: ぐったりする = とても疲れて力がない: worn out, limp.

s: 社長に新商品のアイデアを出したが、ありふれた案だと言われてしまった。
en: I pitched a new product idea to the company president, but was told it was a run-of-the-mill idea.
why: ありふれた means common, nothing special: どこにでもある (found anywhere) says it plainly.
お金のかかる means expensive. ありふれた is about being ordinary, not about cost.
実現が難しい means hard to carry out. An ordinary idea is usually easy to carry out.
わかりにくい means hard to understand. Ordinary ideas are usually easy to follow.
tell: ありふれた = どこにでもある／珍しくない: ordinary, commonplace.

s: 引っ越しのときに、祖父が使っていた頑丈な机を譲ってもらった。
en: When I moved house, I was given the sturdy desk my grandfather used to use.
why: 頑丈 means solid and hard to break: 丈夫 is the everyday word for the same thing.
高価 means expensive. A sturdy desk can be cheap.
便利 means handy or convenient. That is about use, not strength.
おしゃれ means stylish. It is about looks, not how strong it is.
tell: 頑丈な = 丈夫な: strongly built, hard to break.

s: 部長は、新しく取引を始める会社を慎重に選んでいるようだ。
en: The manager seems to be choosing very carefully which new company to do business with.
why: 慎重 means careful, taking time to avoid mistakes: 注意深く (carefully) is the plain version.
一人で means alone. 慎重 is about how carefully, not who decides.
急いで means in a hurry, close to the opposite of 慎重に.
楽しそうに describes mood. 慎重 says nothing about enjoying it.
tell: 慎重に = 注意深く／よく考えて: carefully, to avoid mistakes.

s: 新しい企画について、皆さんの率直な意見を聞かせてください。
en: Please give me your honest opinions on the new project.
why: 率直 means frank, saying what you really think: 正直な (honest) is the plain word.
詳しい means detailed. A frank opinion can be one short sentence.
前向きな means positive. A frank opinion may well be negative.
専門的な means technical or expert. 率直 is about honesty, not expertise.
tell: 率直な = 正直な／遠慮のない: frank, holding nothing back.

s: 専門家の多くは、今回の値上げを妥当な判断だと見ている。
en: Most experts see this price rise as a reasonable decision.
why: 妥当 means reasonable and right for the situation: 適切な says it in plainer words.
大胆な means bold, taking a risk. A reasonable decision is usually not a bold one.
意外な means surprising. 妥当 is about being sensible, not about surprise.
厳しい means harsh or strict. 妥当 says the decision fits the facts, not that it is tough.
tell: 妥当な = 適切な／もっともな: reasonable, fits the situation.

s: 兄は器用で、壊れたいすや棚もすぐに自分で直してしまう。
en: My older brother is good with his hands, and quickly fixes broken chairs and shelves himself.
c: お金を使いたがらなくて
why: 器用 means skilful with your hands: 細かい作業が得意 (good at fine work) says it plainly.
せっかち means impatient. It could explain fixing things at once, but it is not about skill.
お金を使いたがらない means stingy. It could explain not paying for repairs, but it is not about skill.
力が強い means physically strong. 器用 is about fine skill, not strength.
tell: 器用 = 手先が上手／細かい作業が得意: good with your hands.

s: 初めて会う取引先との会議では、余計なことは言わないほうがいい。
en: In a first meeting with a new client, it is better not to say anything unnecessary.
why: 余計 means more than is needed: 必要のない (unnecessary) is the plain version.
難しい means difficult. 余計なこと can be very simple.
個人的な means personal or private. 余計 is about not being needed, whatever the topic.
失礼な means rude. Something unnecessary is not always rude.
tell: 余計な = 必要のない／余分な: more than is needed.

s: 医師によると、この年齢でこの病気になるのはまれなケースだそうだ。
en: According to the doctor, getting this illness at this age is a rare case.
why: まれ means rare, hardly ever happening: めったにない says it plainly.
よくある means common, the opposite of まれ.
難しい means difficult. A rare case is not always a hard one.
危険な means dangerous. まれ is about how often, not how serious.
tell: まれな = めったにない: rare, hardly ever seen.

s: 明日の朝の会議に間に合うように、今夜中にこの報告書を仕上げるつもりだ。
en: I plan to finish this report tonight so it is ready for tomorrow morning's meeting.
why: 仕上げる means to finish something off, to complete it: 完成させる says that plainly.
読み直す means to read again. You can reread a report that is not finished.
印刷する means to print. Printing is not the same as finishing the writing.
提出する means to hand in. You finish a report first, then hand it in.
tell: 仕上げる = 完成させる: finish off, complete.

m: to hold off, put on hold
s: 雨の予報が出ていたので、週末のバーベキューは見合わせることにした。
en: Rain was forecast, so we decided to hold off on the weekend barbecue.
why: 見合わせる means to hold off and not go ahead for now: やめておく says it plainly. Train notices use it too: 運転を見合わせています.
早めに始める means starting earlier. The barbecue would still go ahead.
屋根の下でする means moving it under a roof. It would still go ahead.
少人数でする means doing it with fewer people. It would still go ahead.
tell: 見合わせる = やめておく／しばらく止める: hold off for now.

m: to order in, have something sent
s: 近くの店には置いていなかったので、ネットで北海道のチーズを取り寄せた。
en: The shops nearby did not stock it, so I ordered some Hokkaido cheese online.
c: 注文して送ってもらった
why: 取り寄せる means to order something and have it sent to you: 注文して送ってもらう spells it out.
探して見つける means to search and find. Finding it online is not the same as having it sent.
見比べて選ぶ means to compare and pick. That is a step before ordering, not the ordering itself.
調べて買いに行く means you look it up, then go to buy it. With 取り寄せる it comes to you.
tell: 取り寄せる = 注文して送ってもらう: order in, have it delivered.

m: to cut off, call off partway
s: 両社の交渉は三時間に及んだが、結論が出ないまま打ち切られた。
en: Talks between the two companies went on for three hours, but were called off without a conclusion.
why: 打ち切る means to stop something partway and not continue: 中止する is the plain word.
延長する means to make it run longer, the opposite of cutting it off.
翌日も続けられた means the talks went on the next day, so they did not end.
休憩に入る means to take a break. After a break, the talks carry on.
tell: 打ち切る = 途中でやめる／中止する: cut off, call off.

s: 弟は、リビングの花瓶を割ったのは自分ではないと言い張った。
en: My younger brother insisted that he was not the one who broke the vase in the living room.
why: 言い張る means to keep insisting and refuse to back down: 強く言い続ける says that plainly.
小さな声で言う means saying it quietly. 言い張る is forceful and repeated.
嘘をつく means to lie. 言い張る says nothing about whether it is true.
母に話す means telling your mother. 言い張る is about how firmly you say it, not who hears.
tell: 言い張る = 強く言い続ける: insist, refuse to back down.

m: to pay for someone, to be paid back later
s: 「ホテル代はどうした？」「とりあえず私が四人分まとめて立て替えておいたよ。」
en: What did you do about the hotel bill? For now, I covered it for all four of us.
why: 立て替える means to pay for someone for now, expecting to be paid back: 代わりに払う says that. おごる would mean no payback.
集める means to collect money from people. The money moves the other way.
計算する means to work out the amount. No money changes hands.
確認する means to check it. Nothing is paid.
tell: 立て替える = 代わりに払っておく, and get the money back later.

m: to make a point of, keep in mind
s: 健康のために、エレベーターではなく階段を使うように心がけている。
en: For my health, I make a point of taking the stairs instead of the lift.
why: 心がける means to keep something in mind and make an effort to do it: 気をつけている is the plain version.
言われている means someone has told you to. 心がける is your own effort.
勧めている means you recommend it to other people. 心がける is about yourself.
頼んでいる means you are asking someone else to do it. 心がける is your own habit.
tell: 〜ように心がける = 〜ように気をつける: make a point of doing it.

s: 体調を崩したので、来週の歯医者の予約をキャンセルした。
en: I was not feeling well, so I cancelled my dentist appointment for next week.
why: キャンセルする means to call off a booking: 取り消す is the Japanese word for it.
変更する means to change it, for example to another day. The booking still exists.
確認する means to check or confirm it. The booking stays.
予約を入れる means to make a booking, the opposite.
tell: キャンセルする = 取り消す: call off a booking.

s: 最近、若い人の間で、昔ながらの喫茶店巡りがちょっとしたブームになっている。
en: Lately, visiting old-style coffee shops has become something of a craze among young people.
why: ブーム means a boom or craze, something suddenly popular with many people: 流行 is the Japanese word.
問題 means a problem. A craze is about popularity, not trouble.
息抜き means a short break to relax. That is why someone might do it, not the fact that many people do.
ぜいたく means a luxury or treat. It is about cost, not popularity.
tell: ブーム = 流行: a craze, something suddenly popular.

s: 台風の影響で、市内の工場では生産が一時ストップしている。
en: Because of the typhoon, production at factories in the city has temporarily stopped.
why: ストップする means to stop: 止まる is the plain Japanese word. Nothing is being made for now.
遅れる means to fall behind schedule. Production is still going on.
減る means to go down. Some production is still going on.
混乱する means to be thrown into confusion. Things are disrupted, but not stopped.
tell: ストップする = 止まる／止める: stop, come to a halt.

m: the circumstances, how something came about
s: 新しく来た部長に、プロジェクトが中止になったいきさつを説明した。
en: I explained to the new manager how the project came to be cancelled.
why: いきさつ means how something came about, the chain of events behind it: 事情 (the circumstances) is the closest plain word here. The exact synonym is 経緯 (けいい), and いきさつ is often written 経緯.
結果 means the result, what came after. いきさつ is what came before.
影響 means the effect on other things. That also comes after the event.
時期 means when it happened. いきさつ is the story of how, not the date.
tell: いきさつ = 事情／経緯: how it came to this, the background story.

s: 週末のセールに行ってみたら、案の定、店の中は人でいっぱいだった。
en: I went to the weekend sale and, just as I expected, the shop was packed.
why: 案の定 means 'just as I thought', usually about something unwelcome: 思ったとおり is the plain version.
意外にも means 'surprisingly', the opposite of 案の定.
珍しく means 'unusually, for once'. 案の定 means it was exactly what you expected.
なぜか means 'for some reason'. 案の定 means you saw it coming.
tell: 案の定 = 思ったとおり／予想どおり: just as feared.
